## Proposition 1.1
**Statement:** On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given finite straight line. It is required to construct an equilateral triangle on AB.

**Step 2.** With centre A and distance AB, describe circle BCD. [P3]

**Step 3.** With centre B and distance BA, describe circle ACE. [P3]

**Step 4.** From the point C, in which the circles cut one another, draw the straight lines CA and CB to the points A and B. [P1]

**Step 5.** Since A is the centre of circle BCD, the segment AC is equal to AB. [D1.15]

**Step 6.** Since B is the centre of circle ACE, the segment BC is equal to BA. [D1.15]

**Step 7.** From Steps 5 and 6, both CA and CB are equal to AB. But things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another, so CA is equal to CB. [CN1]

**Step 8.** Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, and BC are equal to one another, and the triangle ABC is equilateral. [D1.20]

**Step 9.** Thus, an equilateral triangle ABC has been constructed on the given finite straight line AB, which is what was required to do.

## Proposition 1.2
**Statement:** To place at a given point (as an extremity) a straight line equal to a given straight line.

**Step 1.** Let A be the given point and BC the given straight line. We must place at A a straight line equal to BC.

**Step 2.** Join A to B by drawing the straight line AB [P1].

**Step 3.** On the straight line AB, construct an equilateral triangle DAB [1.1]. Then DA = DB = AB.

**Step 4.** With centre B and radius BC, describe the circle CGH [P3].

**Step 5.** Produce the straight line DB beyond B to meet the circle CGH at the point G [P2].

**Step 6.** With centre D and radius DG, describe the circle GKL [P3].

**Step 7.** Produce the straight line DA beyond A to meet the circle GKL at the point L [P2].

**Step 8.** Since B is the centre of circle CGH, we have BG = BC [D1.15].

**Step 9.** Since D is the centre of circle GKL, we have DL = DG [D1.15].

**Step 10.** Since triangle DAB is equilateral, DA = DB [by construction in Step 3].

**Step 11.** Since DL = DG and DA = DB, subtracting equals from equals gives AL = BG [CN3]. (For DL - DA = DG - DB, that is, AL = BG.)

**Step 12.** Since BG = BC (Step 8) and AL = BG (Step 11), we conclude AL = BC [CN1].

**Step 13.** Therefore the straight line AL, placed at the given point A as an extremity, is equal to the given straight line BC. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.3
**Statement:** Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the less.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the greater straight line and C the lesser. We are required to cut off from AB a straight line equal to C.

**Step 2.** By Proposition 1.2, place at the point A a straight line AD equal to C, so that AD = C. [1.2]

**Step 3.** With centre A and distance AD, describe the circle DEF. [P3]

**Step 4.** Since A is the centre of circle DEF, AE is a radius of this circle, and AD is also a radius. By Definition 1.15, all straight lines falling from the centre upon the circumference are equal, so AE = AD. [D1.15]

**Step 5.** But AD = C (by Step 2). Since AE = AD and AD = C, by Common Notion 1 we have AE = C. [CN1]

**Step 6.** The point E lies on the straight line AB (since AB is greater than C, the circle intersects AB between A and B), so AE has been cut off from the greater straight line AB, and AE equals the lesser straight line C.

Therefore, given two unequal straight lines, from the greater a straight line equal to the less has been cut off, which is what was required to do. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.4
**Statement:** If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB and AC equal to the two sides DE and DF respectively, namely AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF. We claim that the base BC is equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles are equal, namely angle ABC equals angle DEF and angle ACB equals angle DFE.

**Step 2.** Apply triangle ABC to triangle DEF by placing point A on point D and the straight line AB along DE. Since AB is equal to DE, point B will coincide with point E. [CN4]

**Step 3.** Since AB coincides with DE and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF, the straight line AC will also lie along DF. Since AC is equal to DF, point C will coincide with point F. [CN4]

**Step 4.** Since point B coincides with E and point C coincides with F, the base BC will coincide with the base EF. For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with EF, then two straight lines will enclose a space, which is impossible. Therefore BC coincides with EF and is equal to it. [P1, CN4]

**Step 5.** Since the whole triangle ABC coincides with the whole triangle DEF, the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF. [CN4]

**Step 6.** Since the sides about angle ABC coincide with the sides about angle DEF, the angle ABC is equal to the angle DEF. Similarly, since the sides about angle ACB coincide with the sides about angle DFE, the angle ACB is equal to the angle DFE. [CN4]

**Step 7.** Therefore, if two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.5
**Statement:** In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be an isosceles triangle with AB equal to AC. Produce AB beyond B to an arbitrary point D, and produce AC beyond C to an arbitrary point E. [P2]

**Step 2.** On AD, take an arbitrary point F beyond B. Using Proposition 1.3, cut off from AE a straight line AG equal to AF, so that AF equals AG. [1.3]

**Step 3.** Join FC and GB. [P1]

**Step 4.** Since AF equals AG (by construction in Step 2), and AB equals AC (given, by D1.20), and the angle FAC is common to triangles AFC and AGB (that is, the angle at A is the same angle BAC contained between the respective equal sides), therefore by Proposition 1.4 (SAS), triangle AFC is equal to triangle AGB, and the base FC equals the base GB, and angle ACF equals angle ABG, and angle AFC equals angle AGB. [1.4]

**Step 5.** Since AF equals AG, and AB equals AC, subtracting equals from equals gives BF equals CG. [CN3]

**Step 6.** Now in triangles BFC and CGB: BF equals CG (Step 5), FC equals GB (Step 4), and angle BFC equals angle CGB (Step 4, since angle AFC equals angle AGB, and these are the same angles). Therefore by Proposition 1.4 (SAS), triangle BFC is equal to triangle CGB, and angle FBC equals angle GCB, and angle BCF equals angle CBG. [1.4]

**Step 7.** From Step 4, angle ABG equals angle ACF. From Step 6, angle CBG equals angle BCF. Subtracting equals from equals (angle CBG from angle ABG, and angle BCF from angle ACF), the remainders are equal: angle ABC equals angle ACB. These are the angles at the base of triangle ABC. [CN3]

**Step 8.** From Step 6, angle FBC equals angle GCB. These are the angles under the base. [1.4]

**Step 9.** Therefore, in isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and the equal straight lines having been produced further, the angles under the base are equal to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.6
**Statement:** If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles will also be equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle having angle ABC equal to angle ACB. I say that side AB is also equal to side AC.

**Step 2.** Suppose AB is not equal to AC. Then one of them is greater. Let AB be greater than AC.

**Step 3.** From the greater line AB, cut off DB equal to the lesser AC [1.3].

**Step 4.** Join DC [P1].

**Step 5.** Now in triangles DBC and ACB, we have DB equal to AC (by construction), BC is common to both triangles, and angle DBC is equal to angle ACB (since angle DBC is the same angle as angle ABC, which equals angle ACB by hypothesis).

**Step 6.** Therefore, by the side-angle-side criterion, triangle DBC is equal to triangle ACB [1.4].

**Step 7.** But triangle DBC is a part of triangle ACB, so a part would be equal to the whole. This contradicts the common notion that the whole is greater than the part [CN5].

**Step 8.** Therefore the assumption that AB is not equal to AC is false. Hence AB equals AC.

**Step 9.** Therefore, if in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles will also be equal to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.7
**Statement:** Given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a point, there cannot be constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a given straight line, and let two straight lines AC and BC be constructed on AB from its extremities A and B, meeting at the point C. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that two other straight lines AD and BD can be constructed on AB from the same extremities A and B, on the same side of AB, meeting at a different point D, such that AD = AC and BD = BC.

**Step 2.** Join CD [P1].

**Step 3.** Consider first the case where D falls inside the triangle ACB. Since AC = AD, the triangle ACD is isosceles. Therefore, by 1.5, the angles under the base of triangle ACD, namely angle DCA and angle DCA's counterpart angle CDA (more precisely, the base angles at C and D in triangle ACD) are equal. Specifically, angle ACD = angle ADC [1.5].

**Step 4.** Now, angle BCD is greater than angle ACD, since angle ACD is a part of angle BCD and the whole is greater than the part [CN5]. Therefore angle BCD is greater than angle ADC.

**Step 5.** Since BC = BD, the triangle BCD is also isosceles. Therefore, by 1.5, angle BDC = angle BCD [1.5].

**Step 6.** But from Step 4, angle BCD is greater than angle ADC. Since angle BDC = angle BCD (Step 5), it follows that angle BDC is also greater than angle ADC.

**Step 7.** However, angle ADC is the whole angle at D in triangle ACD with respect to the line CD, and angle BDC is a part of angle ADC (since D is inside triangle ACB, the ray DB falls between DA and DC). Therefore angle ADC is greater than angle BDC [CN5].

**Step 8.** This is a contradiction: Step 6 concluded that angle BDC is greater than angle ADC, while Step 7 concluded that angle ADC is greater than angle BDC. Both cannot hold simultaneously.

**Step 9.** Now consider the case where D falls on the side AC. Then AD is a part of AC, so AD is less than AC [CN5]. But this contradicts the hypothesis that AC = AD. The same argument applies if D falls on BC.

**Step 10.** The case where D falls outside triangle ACB (but still on the same side of AB) is handled similarly to the interior case. When D is exterior, join CD [P1]. Since AC = AD, triangle ACD is isosceles, so by 1.5, the angles under the base CD are equal: that is, the angle under the base at C (angle FCD, where F is on AC produced) equals the angle under the base at D (angle CDG, where G is on AD produced) [1.5, P2]. Now angle BCD is less than angle FCD (since angle BCD is a part of the angle on the other side), but we still have angle FCD = angle GDC. Since BC = BD, triangle BCD is isosceles, so angle BDC = angle BCD [1.5]. Then angle BDC is less than angle GDC. But angle GDC is less than angle BDC (since GDC is a part of BDC when D is exterior), giving the same contradiction.

**Step 11.** In all cases a contradiction arises. Therefore it is impossible to construct on the same straight line, from its extremities and on the same side, two other straight lines equal respectively to the original two and meeting at a different point. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.8
**Statement:** If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal straight lines.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles such that AB = DE, AC = DF, and BC = EF. We wish to show that angle BAC = angle EDF.

**Step 2.** Apply triangle DEF to triangle ABC so that point E is placed on B and the straight line EF is placed along BC. Since EF = BC, point F will coincide with C [CN4].

**Step 3.** With EF coinciding with BC, point D must fall either on the same side of BC as A, or on the opposite side. Since we may choose the application to place D on the same side as A (as both triangles have their vertices on a definite side of their respective bases), suppose D is placed on the same side of BC as A.

**Step 4.** Now suppose D does not coincide with A. Then from point B two straight lines BD and BA are constructed on the same side of BC, and from point C two straight lines CD and CA are constructed on the same side of BC, with BD meeting BA at D and A respectively. We have BD = BA (since BD = DE = AB) and CD = CA (since CD = DF = AC).

**Step 5.** But by Proposition 1.7, given two straight lines BA and CA constructed on BC from its extremities and meeting at A, there cannot be constructed on the same straight line BC, from the same extremities and on the same side, two other straight lines BD and CD meeting at another point D with BD = BA and CD = CA. This is a contradiction [1.7].

**Step 6.** Therefore the supposition that D does not coincide with A is false. Point D must coincide with A.

**Step 7.** Since D coincides with A, the straight line DE coincides with AB and the straight line DF coincides with AC. Therefore angle EDF coincides with angle BAC, and hence angle EDF = angle BAC [CN4].

**Step 8.** Therefore, if two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively and have the base equal to the base, they also have equal the angles contained by the equal straight lines. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.9
**Statement:** To bisect a given rectilineal angle.

**Step 1.** Let the angle BAC be the given rectilineal angle. It is required to bisect it.

**Step 2.** Take an arbitrary point D on the ray AB [by choosing any point on AB other than A].

**Step 3.** Using Proposition 1.3, cut off from AC a straight line AE equal to AD, so that AE = AD.

**Step 4.** Join D to E by a straight line [P1].

**Step 5.** On the straight line DE, construct an equilateral triangle DEF on the side of DE away from A [1.1].

**Step 6.** Join A to F by a straight line [P1].

**Step 7.** Now consider triangles ADF and AEF. We have: AD = AE (by construction in Step 3); DF = EF (since triangle DEF is equilateral, so all its sides are equal); and AF is common to both triangles.

**Step 8.** Since the two triangles ADF and AEF have the three sides equal to the three sides respectively (AD = AE, DF = EF, AF = AF), by Proposition 1.8 (SSS congruence) the angles contained by the equal sides are equal. In particular, angle DAF = angle EAF.

**Step 9.** Since angle DAF = angle EAF, and these two angles together compose the original angle BAC, the straight line AF bisects the given rectilineal angle BAC.

**Step 10.** Therefore the given rectilineal angle BAC has been bisected by the straight line AF, which is what was required to do. Q.E.F.

**Statement:** To bisect a given finite straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given finite straight line. It is required to bisect it.

**Step 2.** Construct an equilateral triangle ABC on AB [1.1].

**Step 3.** Since triangle ABC is equilateral, we have AC = BC [D1.20, 1.1].

**Step 4.** Bisect the angle ACB by the straight line CD, where D is the point at which CD meets AB [1.9].

**Step 5.** Consider triangles ACD and BCD. We have: AC = BC [Step 3]; the angle ACD = angle BCD [Step 4, by construction via 1.9]; and CD is common to both triangles.

**Step 6.** Since the two triangles ACD and BCD have two sides equal to two sides respectively (AC = BC and CD = CD), and the angles contained by those equal sides are equal (angle ACD = angle BCD), by Proposition 1.4 the remaining parts are also equal. In particular, the base AD = the base DB [1.4].

**Step 7.** Therefore the given finite straight line AB has been bisected at the point D, which is what was required to do.

## Proposition 1.11
**Statement:** To draw a straight line at right angles to a given straight line from a given point on it.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line and C the given point on it. We are required to draw a straight line from C at right angles to AB.

**Step 2.** Take an arbitrary point D on AC (that is, on AB on one side of C). [No axiom needed; D is simply chosen on the given line.]

**Step 3.** Using Proposition 1.3, cut off from CB a segment CE equal to CD, so that CD = CE. [1.3]

**Step 4.** On the segment DE, construct an equilateral triangle DEF, using Proposition 1.1. Then DF = EF (since triangle DEF is equilateral). [1.1]

**Step 5.** Join the straight line FC, by Postulate 1. [P1]

**Step 6.** Now consider triangles DCF and ECF. We have: DC = EC (by Step 3), CF is common to both triangles, and DF = EF (by Step 4, since DEF is equilateral). Therefore, by Proposition 1.8 (if two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively, and the base equal to the base, then the angles contained by the equal sides are equal), angle DCF equals angle ECF. [1.8]

**Step 7.** But these angles DCF and ECF are adjacent angles formed by the straight line CF standing on the straight line AB at the point C. Since these adjacent angles are equal to one another, each of them is a right angle, and the straight line CF is perpendicular to AB, by Definition 1.10. [D1.10]

**Step 8.** Therefore, the straight line CF has been drawn at right angles to the given straight line AB from the given point C on it, which is what was required to be done.

## Proposition 1.12
**Statement:** To a given infinite straight line, from a given point which is not on it, to draw a perpendicular straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given infinite straight line, and let C be the given point which is not on it. It is required to draw from the point C a straight line perpendicular to the straight line AB.

**Step 2.** Let a point D be taken at random on the other side of AB from C. With centre C and distance CD, describe the circle EGD [P3]. Since C is not on line AB and the circle has radius reaching to the other side of AB, the circle meets the straight line AB at two points; call them G and E.

**Step 3.** Bisect the straight line GE at the point H [1.10].

**Step 4.** Join the straight lines CG, CH, and CE [P1].

**Step 5.** Now, since GH is equal to HE (for H is the midpoint of GE by construction in Step 3), and HC is common to the triangles GHC and EHC, the two sides GH, HC are equal to the two sides EH, HC respectively.

**Step 6.** Moreover, CG is equal to CE, since both are radii of the circle EGD with centre C [D1.15].

**Step 7.** Therefore triangle GHC has the two sides GH, HC equal to two sides EH, HC of triangle EHC respectively, and the base CG is equal to the base CE. By Proposition 1.8 (if two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively and the base equal to the base, the angles contained by the equal straight lines are equal), the angle CHG is equal to the angle CHE [1.8].

**Step 8.** But the angles CHG and CHE are adjacent angles formed by the straight line CH standing on the straight line GE. Since these adjacent angles are equal to one another, each of them is a right angle, and the straight line CH is called a perpendicular to GE [D1.10].

**Step 9.** Therefore, from the given point C, which is not on the given infinite straight line AB, a perpendicular CH has been drawn to AB. This is what was required to do.

## Proposition 1.13
**Statement:** If a straight line set up on a straight line make angles, it will make either two right angles or angles equal to two right angles.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be given, and let the straight line CD be set up on it at the point C, making the angles ACD and BCD. We must show that the angles ACD and BCD are either two right angles or together equal to two right angles.

**Step 2.** (Case 1) If the angle ACD equals the angle BCD, then since the straight line CD set up on the straight line AB makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the angles ACD and BCD is a right angle by Definition D1.10. Therefore the angles ACD and BCD together make two right angles.

**Step 3.** (Case 2) Suppose the angle ACD is not equal to the angle BCD. Draw CE from the point C at right angles to the straight line AB, by Proposition 1.11. Then each of the angles ACE and BCE is a right angle, and so the angles ACE and BCE together equal two right angles.

**Step 4.** Now the angle ACE is the whole, and the angle ACD is a part of it, so the angle ACE equals the sum of the angles ACD and DCE. Adding the angle BCE to each side, the angles ACE and BCE together equal the angles ACD, DCE, and BCE together, by Common Notion CN2.

**Step 5.** Similarly, the angle BCD is the whole, and the angle BCE is a part of it, so the angle BCD equals the sum of the angles BCE and DCE. Adding the angle ACD to each side, the angles ACD and BCD together equal the angles ACD, DCE, and BCE together, by Common Notion CN2.

**Step 6.** But the angles ACE and BCE together were shown to also equal the angles ACD, DCE, and BCE together (Step 4). Therefore the angles ACD and BCD together equal the angles ACE and BCE together, by Common Notion CN1.

**Step 7.** But the angles ACE and BCE together equal two right angles (Step 3). Therefore the angles ACD and BCD together equal two right angles.

**Step 8.** Hence in either case, the straight line CD set up on the straight line AB makes the angles ACD and BCD either two right angles or angles together equal to two right angles, which was to be proved.

## Proposition 1.14
**Statement:** If with any straight line, and at a point on it, two straight lines not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles, the two straight lines will be in a straight line with one another.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line, and let B be a point on it. Let two straight lines BC and BD, not lying on the same side of AB, make the adjacent angles ABC and ABD together equal to two right angles. We claim that BD is in a straight line with BC.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that BD is not in a straight line with BC. Then produce the straight line CB beyond B to a point E, so that BE is the continuation of CB in a straight line [P2].

**Step 3.** Since the straight line AB stands on the straight line CBE, by Proposition 1.13, the angles ABC and ABE together equal two right angles [1.13].

**Step 4.** But by hypothesis, the angles ABC and ABD together also equal two right angles. Therefore the sum of angles ABC and ABE equals the sum of angles ABC and ABD [CN1].

**Step 5.** Subtract the common angle ABC from each sum. Then the remaining angle ABE equals the remaining angle ABD [CN3].

**Step 6.** But the angle ABE is greater than the angle ABD, since ABD is a part of ABE (because BD falls between BA and BE, given that BD does not coincide with BE by our assumption). This means the whole equals the part, which is impossible [CN5].

**Step 7.** Therefore the assumption is false: BD is not not in a straight line with BC. Hence BD is in a straight line with BC, which was to be proved.

## Proposition 1.15
**Statement:** If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let the two straight lines AB and CD cut one another at the point E. I say that the angle AEC is equal to the angle DEB, and the angle CEB is equal to the angle AED.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AE stands on the straight line CD, making the angles AEC and AED, by Proposition 1.13 the angles AEC and AED together equal two right angles.

**Step 3.** Again, since the straight line DE stands on the straight line AB, making the angles AED and DEB, by Proposition 1.13 the angles AED and DEB together equal two right angles.

**Step 4.** But the angles AEC and AED were also shown equal to two right angles. Therefore the sum of angles AEC and AED equals the sum of angles AED and DEB, since things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another (CN1).

**Step 5.** Subtract the angle AED from each sum. By Common Notion 3, the remainders are equal; therefore the angle AEC equals the angle DEB.

**Step 6.** Similarly, since the straight line BE stands on the straight line CD, by Proposition 1.13 the angles DEB and CEB together equal two right angles. And the angles DEB and AED were also shown equal to two right angles (Step 3). Therefore the sum of angles DEB and CEB equals the sum of angles DEB and AED, by CN1.

**Step 7.** Subtract the angle DEB from each sum. By Common Notion 3, the angle CEB equals the angle AED.

**Step 8.** Therefore, if two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.16
**Statement:** In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, and let the side BC be produced to D. We shall prove that the exterior angle ACD is greater than each of the interior and opposite angles, namely angle BAC and angle ABC.

**Step 2.** Bisect AC at E [1.10]. Join B to E by a straight line [P1].

**Step 3.** Produce the straight line BE in a straight line to F [P2], and cut off EF equal to BE [1.3]. Join F to C by a straight line [P1].

**Step 4.** In triangles AEB and CEF, we have AE = EC (since E is the midpoint of AC by Step 2), BE = EF (by construction in Step 3), and angle AEB = angle CEF (since they are vertical angles formed by lines AC and BF cutting one another at E) [1.15].

## Proposition 1.18
**Statement:** In any triangle the greater side subtends the greater angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle in which side AC is greater than side AB. We must show that angle ABC (the angle subtended by the greater side AC) is greater than angle ACB (the angle subtended by the lesser side AB).

**Step 2.** Since AC is greater than AB, by Proposition 1.3 we may cut off from AC a straight line AD equal to AB, so that D lies on AC between A and C.

**Step 3.** Join B to D by Postulate 1.

**Step 4.** In triangle ABD, since AB equals AD (by construction in Step 2), triangle ABD is isosceles. Therefore by Proposition 1.5, angle ABD equals angle ADB.

**Step 5.** Now consider triangle BDC. Since D lies between A and C, the segment CD is a side of triangle BDC. If side CD is produced beyond D to A, then angle BDA is an exterior angle of triangle BDC. By Proposition 1.16, this exterior angle BDA is greater than the interior and opposite angle BCD.

**Step 6.** But angle BCD is the same as angle ACB (since D lies on segment AC, so C sees B from the same angle whether we call it BCD or ACB). Therefore angle BDA is greater than angle ACB.

**Step 7.** Since angle ABD equals angle ADB (Step 4), and angle ADB equals angle BDA (they are the same angle), we have angle ABD is greater than angle ACB.

**Step 8.** Now, since D lies between A and C, the ray BD lies within angle ABC, so angle ABD is a part of angle ABC. By Common Notion 5, the whole is greater than the part, hence angle ABC is greater than angle ABD.

**Step 9.** Since angle ABC is greater than angle ABD (Step 8), and angle ABD is greater than angle ACB (Step 7), it follows that angle ABC is greater than angle ACB.

**Step 10.** Therefore, in triangle ABC, the greater side AC subtends the greater angle ABC, which is what was to be proved.

## Proposition 1.19
**Statement:** In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle in which angle ABC is greater than angle BCA. We must show that side AC (which subtends angle ABC) is greater than side AB (which subtends angle BCA).

**Step 2.** There are exactly three possibilities: either AC equals AB, or AC is less than AB, or AC is greater than AB.

**Step 3.** Suppose AC equals AB. Then triangle ABC is isosceles with AC equal to AB. By 1.5, the angles at the base are equal, so angle ABC equals angle BCA. But this contradicts the hypothesis that angle ABC is greater than angle BCA. Therefore AC does not equal AB.

**Step 4.** Suppose AC is less than AB. Then AB is greater than AC. Since AB is the greater side in triangle ABC, by 1.18, the angle subtended by the greater side AB is greater than the angle subtended by the lesser side AC. That is, angle ACB is greater than angle ABC. But this contradicts the hypothesis that angle ABC is greater than angle BCA. Therefore AC is not less than AB.

**Step 5.** Since AC is neither equal to AB nor less than AB, it follows that AC is greater than AB. Therefore the greater angle ABC is subtended by the greater side AC, which is what was to be proved.

## Proposition 1.21
**Statement:** If on one of the sides of a triangle, from its extremities, there be constructed two straight lines meeting within the triangle, the straight lines so constructed will be less than the remaining two sides of the triangle, but will contain a greaterangle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, and from the extremities B and C of side BC, let two straight lines BD and DC be constructed meeting at a point D within the triangle. We are to prove that BD + DC < BA + AC, and that angle BDC > angle BAC.

**Step 2.** Produce BD beyond D. Since D is within triangle ABC, the line BD produced will meet side AC at some point. Let it meet AC at E [P1, P2]. Then B, D, E are collinear with D between B and E, and E lies on AC with A-E-C (E is between A and C).

**Step 3.** In triangle ABE, since any two sides taken together are greater than the remaining one [1.20], we have BA + AE > BE.

**Step 4.** Adding EC to both sides [CN2], we obtain BA + AE + EC > BE + EC. Since E lies on segment AC, we have AE + EC = AC. Therefore BA + AC > BE + EC.

**Step 5.** In triangle DEC, since any two sides taken together are greater than the remaining one [1.20], we have DE + EC > DC.

**Step 6.** Adding BD to both sides [CN2], we obtain BD + DE + EC > BD + DC. Since D lies on segment BE, we have BD + DE = BE. Therefore BE + EC > BD + DC.

**Step 7.** From Step 4, BA + AC > BE + EC, and from Step 6, BE + EC > BD + DC. Therefore BA + AC > BD + DC. That is, the two straight lines BD and DC constructed within the triangle are together less than the remaining two sides BA and AC.

**Step 8.** Now we prove the angle part. Since B, D, E are collinear and D lies between B and E, the angle BDC is an exterior angle of triangle DEC (being the angle at vertex D formed by producing side ED beyond D to B). By 1.16, an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles. Therefore angle BDC > angle DEC.

**Step 9.** Since B, D, E are collinear and E lies on AC between A and C, the angle BEC (which is the same angle as angle DEC, since D lies on ray EB) is an exterior angle of triangle ABE at vertex E, being formed by producing side AE beyond E to C while line BE meets it. By 1.16, angle BEC > angle BAE. But angle BAE is the same as angle BAC. Therefore angle BEC > angle BAC.

**Step 10.** From Step 8, angle BDC > angle DEC. Since D lies on segment BE, angle DEC and angle BEC are the same angle. Therefore angle BDC > angle BEC > angle BAC, which gives angle BDC > angle BAC.

**Step 11.** Therefore the straight lines BD, DC constructed on side BC and meeting within the triangle are together less than the remaining two sides BA, AC, but contain a greater angle. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.22
**Statement:** Out of three straight lines, which are equal to three given straight lines, to construct a triangle: thus it is necessary that two of the straight lines taken together in any manner should be greater than the remaining one.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be three given straight lines such that any two taken together are greater than the remaining one: A + B > C, A + C > B, and B + C > A. We must construct a triangle having its three sides equal to A, B, C respectively.

**Step 2.** Set out a straight line DE, terminated at D but infinite in the direction of E [P2]. Using Proposition 1.3, cut off DF from DE equal to A [1.3]. Then from the remainder, again using 1.3, cut off FG equal to B, and from the remainder cut off GH equal to C. So DF = A, FG = B, GH = C, and D, F, G, H lie in order along the line DE.

**Step 3.** With center F and distance FD, describe a circle DKL [P3]. With center G and distance GH, describe a circle KHL [P3].

**Step 4.** We show the two circles must meet. Since A + B > C, we have DF + FG > GH. Thus FG < DF + FG, so the point D lies on the circle DKL and is at distance FD from F on the side of F away from G; meanwhile G is at distance FG from F, and since FG < FD + FG but also GH < FG + FD (because C < B + A by hypothesis), the circle centered at G with radius GH does not lie entirely outside circle DKL. Conversely, since B + C > A, we have FG + GH > FD, so the circle centered at G with radius GH extends beyond F on the far side, meaning circle DKL does not contain circle KHL entirely within it. Therefore the two circles meet; let them meet at the point K.

**Step 5.** Join KF and KG [P1].

**Step 6.** Since F is the center of circle DKL, and both FD and FK are radii of this circle, we have FK = FD [D1.15]. But DF = A (by construction in Step 2). Therefore FK = A [CN1].

**Step 7.** Since G is the center of circle KHL, and both GH and GK are radii of this circle, we have GK = GH [D1.15]. But GH = C (by construction in Step 2). Therefore GK = C [CN1].

**Step 8.** By construction, FG = B (Step 2).

**Step 9.** Therefore triangle KFG has been constructed with FK = A, FG = B, and GK = C. That is, out of three straight lines FK, FG, GK, which are equal to the three given straight lines A, B, C, a triangle has been constructed. The condition that any two of the given lines taken together are greater than the remaining one (which follows from 1.20 for any triangle) was necessary to ensure the construction succeeds. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.23
**Statement:** On a given straight line and at a point on it to construct a rectilineal angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

**Step 4.** The three straight lines CD, CE, DE satisfy the triangle inequality (since they already form triangle DCE), so by Proposition 1.22, construct a triangle FAG from three straight lines equal to CD, CE, and DE respectively, arranged so that AF = CD, AG = CE, and FG = DE, with vertex A at the given point on line AB [1.22].

**Step 5.** Now in triangles FAG and DCE: AF = CD, AG = CE, and FG = DE. Since the two triangles have their three sides equal to three sides respectively, by Proposition 1.8 (SSS congruence), the angles contained by the equal sides are equal. In particular, angle FAG = angle DCE [1.8].

**Step 6.** Therefore, on the given straight line AB and at the given point A on it, the rectilineal angle FAG has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal angle DCE, which is what was required to do.

## Proposition 1.24
**Statement:** If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other, they will also have the base greater than the base.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, and let the angle BAC be greater than the angle EDF. We must show that BC is greater than EF.

**Step 2.** At the point D on the straight line DE, construct the angle EDG equal to the angle BAC [1.23]. Make DG equal to DF (which equals AC) [1.3]. Join EG and FG [P1].

**Step 3.** Since AB equals DE, and AC equals DG (for AC equals DF and DF equals DG by construction), and the angle BAC equals the angle EDG (by construction), therefore by the side-angle-side congruence, the base BC equals the base EG, and triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEG [1.4].

**Step 4.** Since DG equals DF, triangle DGF is isosceles. Therefore the angle DGF equals the angle DFG [1.5].

**Step 5.** Now the angle DGF is greater than the angle EGF, since the whole is greater than the part [CN5].

**Step 6.** Therefore the angle DFG is also greater than the angle EGF (since angle DFG equals angle DGF by Step 4, and angle DGF is greater than angle EGF by Step 5).

**Step 7.** Moreover, the angle EFG is greater than the angle DFG, since the whole is greater than the part [CN5]. Therefore the angle EFG is even greater than the angle EGF.

**Step 8.** In triangle EFG, since the angle EFG is greater than the angle EGF, the side opposite the greater angle is greater than the side opposite the lesser angle. Therefore EG is greater than EF [1.19].

**Step 9.** But EG equals BC (Step 3). Therefore BC is greater than EF.

**Step 10.** Therefore, if two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other, they will also have the base greater than the base. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.25
**Statement:** If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the base greater than the base, they will also have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, but the base BC greater than the base EF. I say that the angle BAC is greater than the angle EDF.

**Step 2.** For if the angle BAC is not greater than the angle EDF, it is either equal to it or less than it.

**Step 3.** First, suppose the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF. Then, since AB equals DE, AC equals DF, and the angle BAC equals the angle EDF, by Proposition 1.4 (the side-angle-side congruence theorem), the base BC equals the base EF.

**Step 4.** But BC is given as greater than EF. Therefore BC both equals and is greater than EF, which is impossible. Hence the angle BAC is not equal to the angle EDF.

**Step 5.** Next, suppose the angle BAC is less than the angle EDF. Then, since AB equals DE, AC equals DF, and the angle BAC is less than the angle EDF, by Proposition 1.24 (if two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively but the included angle of the first is greater than the included angle of the second, the base of the first is greater than the base of the second), the base EF is greater than the base BC.

**Step 6.** But BC is given as greater than EF. Therefore BC is both greater than and less than EF, which is impossible. Hence the angle BAC is not less than the angle EDF.

**Step 7.** Since the angle BAC is neither equal to nor less than the angle EDF, it remains that the angle BAC is greater than the angle EDF.

**Step 8.** Therefore, if two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the base greater than the base, they will also have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.26
**Statement:** If two triangles have the two angles equal to two angles respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely, either the side adjoining the equal angles, or that subtending one of the equal angles, they will also have the remaining sides equal tothe remaining sides and the remaining angle to the remaining angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles. The proposition has two cases.

CASE 1 (Side adjoining the equal angles): Suppose angle ABC equals angle DEF, angle BCA equals angle EFD, and the side adjoining these angles is equal, namely BC equals EF. We prove that AB equals DE, AC equals DF, and angle BAC equals angle EDF.

**Step 2.** Suppose AB is not equal to DE. Then one of them is greater. Without loss of generality, let AB be greater than DE.

**Step 3.** By Proposition 1.3, cut off from AB a segment BG equal to DE, so that BG equals DE.

**Step 4.** Join GC by Postulate P1.

**Step 5.** In triangles GBC and DEF, we have BG equals DE, BC equals EF, and angle GBC equals angle DEF. Therefore by Proposition 1.4, triangle GBC is congruent to triangle DEF, and angle GCB equals angle DFE.

**Step 6.** But angle DFE equals angle BCA by hypothesis. So angle GCB equals angle BCA by Common Notion CN1.

**Step 7.** Since G lies between A and B on segment AB, angle GCB is a part of angle BCA. But a part cannot equal the whole, by Common Notion CN5. This is a contradiction.

**Step 8.** Therefore AB is not unequal to DE, so AB equals DE.

**Step 9.** Since AB equals DE, BC equals EF, and angle ABC equals angle DEF, by Proposition 1.4, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. Therefore AC equals DF and angle BAC equals angle EDF. This completes Case 1.

CASE 2 (Side subtending one of the equal angles): Suppose angle ABC equals angle DEF, angle BAC equals angle EDF, and the side subtending one of the equal angles is equal, namely BC equals EF (where BC subtends angle BAC and EF subtends angle EDF). We prove that AB equals DE, AC equals DF, and angle BCA equals angle EFD.

**Step 10.** Suppose AB is not equal to DE. Then one of them is greater. Without loss of generality, let AB be greater than DE.

**Step 11.** By Proposition 1.3, cut off from AB a segment BG equal to DE, so that BG equals DE.

**Step 12.** Join GC by Postulate P1.

**Step 13.** In triangles GBC and DEF, we have BG equals DE, BC equals EF, and angle GBC equals angle DEF. Therefore by Proposition 1.4, triangle GBC is congruent to triangle DEF, and angle BGC equals angle EDF.

**Step 14.** But angle EDF equals angle BAC by hypothesis. Therefore angle BGC equals angle BAC by Common Notion CN1.

**Step 15.** Now G lies on segment AB between B and A. In triangle AGC, the angle BGC is an exterior angle formed by producing side AG to B. By Proposition 1.16, this exterior angle BGC must be greater than the interior and opposite angle GAC, which is the same as angle BAC.

**Step 16.** Therefore angle BGC is greater than angle BAC. But Step 14 established that angle BGC equals angle BAC. This is a contradiction.

**Step 17.** Therefore AB is not unequal to DE, so AB equals DE.

**Step 18.** Since AB equals DE, BC equals EF, and angle ABC equals angle DEF, by Proposition 1.4, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. Therefore AC equals DF and angle BCA equals angle EFD. This completes Case 2.

## Proposition 1.27
**Statement:** If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the alternate angles equal to one another, the straight lines will be parallel to one another.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line EF fall on the two straight lines AB and CD, making the alternate angles AEH and GHD equal, where E is the point of intersection with AB and H is the point of intersection with CD. We are to prove that AB is parallel to CD.

**Step 2.** Suppose AB is not parallel to CD. Then, by the definition of parallel lines (D1.23), the lines AB and CD, when produced, will meet on one side or the other.

**Step 3.** Suppose they meet at a point K on the side of B and D when produced. Then E, H, and K form a triangle EHK.

**Step 4.** In triangle EHK, the angle AEH is an exterior angle, since it is formed by side EH of the triangle and the extension EA of side EK beyond vertex E. The angle EHK is an interior and opposite angle of this triangle.

**Step 5.** By Proposition 1.16, the exterior angle of any triangle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles. Therefore angle AEH is greater than angle EHK.

**Step 6.** But angle EHK is the same as angle GHD (since K lies on the extension of CD beyond H in the direction of D, making angle EHK and angle GHD the same angle, or equivalently K is on ray HD so angle EHK = angle GHD). Therefore angle AEH is greater than angle GHD.

**Step 7.** This contradicts the hypothesis that angle AEH equals angle GHD. Therefore AB and CD do not meet on the side of B and D.

**Step 8.** By an entirely symmetric argument, if AB and CD were to meet on the side of A and C at some point K', then in triangle EHK', the angle GHD would be an exterior angle and angle HEA' (i.e., angle BEH, which equals angle AEH's supplement's complement — more precisely, angle DHK' = angle GHD is exterior to triangle EHK' while angle HEK' is interior and opposite). Applying 1.16 again, angle GHD would be greater than angle HEK', that is, greater than angle AEH (since angle HEK' = angle AEH as K' lies on ray EA). This again contradicts the hypothesis that these alternate angles are equal.

**Step 9.** Since AB and CD do not meet when produced in either direction, they are parallel by the definition of parallel lines (D1.23).

**Step 10.** Therefore, if a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the straight lines are parallel to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.28

**Step 3.** By 1.15, the exterior angle EGB is equal to the vertically opposite angle AGH, since EF and AB cut one another at G.

**Step 5.** But angles AGH and GHD are alternate angles formed by the transversal EF falling on the two straight lines AB and CD. Since these alternate angles are equal, by 1.27, AB is parallel to CD.

**Case 2: The interior angles on the same side equal two right angles.**

**Step 6.** Suppose the interior angles on the same side, namely angles BGH and GHD, are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 7.** By 1.13, since EGB and BGH are adjacent angles formed by the straight line GB set up on the straight line EF, the angles EGB and BGH are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 8.** Since angles BGH and GHD together equal two right angles (hypothesis, Step 6), and angles EGB and BGH together equal two right angles (Step 7), by CN1 the sum of angles BGH and GHD equals the sum of angles EGB and BGH.

**Step 11.** Therefore by CN1, angle AGH equals angle GHD.

**Step 12.** But angles AGH and GHD are alternate angles. Since these alternate angles are equal, by 1.27, AB is parallel to CD.

**Step 13.** Therefore, if a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, or the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles, the straight lines are parallel to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.29
**Statement:** A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles.

**Step 1.** Let AB and CD be parallel straight lines, and let the straight line EF fall on them, meeting AB at G and CD at H. We are to show that (i) the alternate angles AGH and GHD are equal, (ii) the exterior angle EGB equals the interior and opposite angle GHD, and (iii) the interior angles on the same side, BGH and GHD, are equal to two right angles.

**Step 2.** (Part i: Alternate angles are equal.) Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that angle AGH is not equal to angle GHD. Then one of them is greater than the other. Suppose angle AGH is greater than angle GHD.

**Step 3.** Add angle BGH to each. Then angle AGH together with angle BGH is greater than angle GHD together with angle BGH.

**Step 4.** But since EGB is a straight line, and the straight line GA stands on it at G, the angles AGH and BGH together equal two right angles [1.13].

**Step 5.** Therefore angle GHD together with angle BGH is less than two right angles.

**Step 8.** But triangle DBC is greater than triangle EBC, the whole greater than the part (by CN5), since E lies on BD or BD produced and is distinct from D, so that one of these triangles contains the other.

**Step 10.** Therefore the assumption that AD is not parallel to BC is false, and AD is parallel to BC.

**Step 6.** Now triangle ABC is composed of triangle AEK, triangle KGC, and the complement EBGK. Likewise, triangle ACD is composed of triangle AHK, triangle KFC, and the complement HKFD.

**Step 8.** Therefore, in any parallelogram the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter are equal to one another, which is what was to be proved.

**Step 6.** We show that GH and HM lie in a straight line. In parallelogram KGHL, the angle GHL (at vertex H) equals the angle GKL (its opposite angle) which equals F [1.34]. Thus angle GHL + angle LHM = F + (two right angles minus F) = two right angles. Therefore by 1.14, GH and HM lie in a straight line.

**Step 7.** We show that HM and MN lie in a straight line. In parallelogram LHMS, the angle HMS (at vertex M) equals the angle HLS (its opposite angle) which equals F [1.34]. In parallelogram SMNP, the angle at S equals F (by construction), so the angle SMN (at vertex M) equals two right angles minus F [1.29, since SP is parallel to MN]. ## Proposition 1.46
**Statement:** On a given straight line to describe a square.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line. It is required to describe a square on AB.

**Step 2.** From the point A, draw AC at right angles to AB [1.11], and on AC cut off AD equal to AB [1.3].

**Step 3.** Through D draw DE parallel to AB [1.31], and through B draw BE parallel to AD [1.31].

**Step 4.** Then ADEB is a parallelogram, so AB is equal to DE and AD is equal to BE [1.34].

**Step 5.** But AD was made equal to AB [Step 2]. Therefore AB, DE, AD, and BE are all equal to one another [CN1].

**Step 6.** Hence the parallelogram ADEB is equilateral.

**Step 7.** Now since AD is parallel to BE, and the straight line AB falls on them, the angles DAB and ABE are interior angles on the same side and therefore sum to two right angles [1.29].

**Step 8.** But the angle DAB is a right angle, since AC (and hence AD, which lies on AC) was drawn at right angles to AB [Step 2, D1.10]. Therefore the angle ABE is also a right angle.

**Step 9.** Since ADEB is a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal [1.34]. Therefore angle ADE is equal to angle ABE, and angle DAB is equal to angle DEB.

**Step 10.** Since angle DAB is a right angle and angle ABE is a right angle, it follows that angle ADE is a right angle and angle DEB is a right angle [Step 9].

**Step 11.** Therefore ADEB is both equilateral and right-angled, and is thus a square by definition [D1.22].

**Step 12.** And it has been described on the given straight line AB. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.47
**Statement:** In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a right-angled triangle having the right angle BAC. We are to show that the square on BC is equal to the sum of the squares on BA and AC.

**Step 3.** Through A, draw AL parallel to BD (or CE), and join AD and FC [1.31, P1].

**Step 4.** Since angle BAC is a right angle (given) and angle BAG is a right angle (since BAGF is a square, by D1.22), the angles BAC and BAG together make two right angles. Therefore CA and AG lie in a straight line [1.14].

**Step 5.** Similarly, since angle BAC is a right angle and angle CAK is a right angle (since ACKH is a square, by D1.22), the angles BAC and CAK together make two right angles. Therefore BA and AK lie in a straight line [1.14].

**Step 6.** Now, since angle DBC is a right angle (BDEC is a square) and angle FBA is a right angle (BAGF is a square), we have angle DBC equal to angle FBA [P4]. Adding angle ABC to each, we get angle DBA equal to angle FBC [CN2].

**Step 7.** In triangles ABD and FBC: AB equals FB (sides of square BAGF), BD equals BC (sides of square BDEC), and angle ABD equals angle FBC (Step 6). Therefore triangle ABD is equal to triangle FBC [1.4].

**Step 8.** Now the parallelogram BL (that is, the rectangle BDLA) has the same base BD as triangle ABD and they are between the same parallels BD and AL. Therefore parallelogram BL is double triangle ABD [1.41].

**Step 9.** The square BAGF has the same base FB as triangle FBC and they are between the same parallels FB and GC (since FB and GC are parallel, as GA is the same straight line as CA by Step 4, and BAGF is a square with FG parallel to BA). Therefore square BAGF is double triangle FBC [1.41].

**Step 10.** But triangle ABD equals triangle FBC (Step 7). Since parallelogram BL is double triangle ABD, and square BAGF is double triangle FBC, and the doubles of equals are equal to one another, therefore parallelogram BL equals square BAGF [CN1].

**Step 11.** Similarly, by joining AE and BK: since angle ECB is a right angle (BDEC is a square) and angle KCA is a right angle (ACKH is a square), angle ACE equals angle BCK [P4]. Adding angle ACB to each, angle BCE equals angle ACK [CN2].

**Step 12.** In triangles BCE and ACK: BC equals CE (sides of square BDEC), AC equals CK (sides of square ACKH), and angle BCE equals angle ACK (Step 11). Therefore triangle BCE equals triangle ACK [1.4].

**Step 13.** The parallelogram CL (that is, the rectangle CELA) has the same base CE as triangle BCE and they are between the same parallels CE and AL. Therefore parallelogram CL is double triangle BCE [1.41].

**Step 14.** The square ACKH has the same base CK as triangle ACK and they are between the same parallels CK and AH (since BA and AK are in a straight line by Step 5, and ACKH is a square with HK parallel to AC). Therefore square ACKH is double triangle ACK [1.41].

**Step 15.** But triangle BCE equals triangle ACK (Step 12). Since parallelogram CL is double triangle BCE, and square ACKH is double triangle ACK, therefore parallelogram CL equals square ACKH [CN1].

**Step 16.** Now the whole square BDEC is composed of the two parallelograms BL and CL. And we have shown that BL equals square BAGF (Step 10) and CL equals square ACKH (Step 15). Therefore the square on BC equals the sum of the squares on BA and AC [CN2].

**Step 17.** Therefore in right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.48
**Statement:** If in a triangle the square on one of the sides be equal to the squares on the remaining two sides of the triangle, the angle contained by the remaining two sides of the triangle is right.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle in which the square on BC is equal to the squares on BA and AC. I say that the angle BAC is right.

**Step 2.** From point A, draw AD at right angles to AC, so that angle DAC is a right angle [1.11]. Make AD equal to BA [1.3].

**Step 3.** Join DC [P1].

**Step 5.** Add to each the square on AC. Then the squares on DA and AC together equal the squares on BA and AC together [CN2].

**Step 6.** Now since the angle DAC is right, the square on DC is equal to the squares on DA and AC [1.47].

**Step 7.** And the square on BC is equal to the squares on BA and AC (by hypothesis).

**Step 8.** Therefore the square on DC is equal to the square on BC [CN1]. Hence DC equals BC.

**Step 9.** Since DA equals AB (by construction), AC is common to triangles DAC and BAC, and the base DC equals the base BC, the two sides DA, AC are equal to the two sides BA, AC respectively, and base equals base.

## Proposition 2.1
**Statement:** If there be two straight lines, and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments.

**Step 1.** Let A and BC be two straight lines, and let BC be cut at any points D and E (the argument generalizes to any number of segments). We must show that the rectangle contained by A and BC equals the sum of the rectangles contained by A and each of the segments BD, DE, and EC.

**Step 2.** From B, draw BF at right angles to BC [1.11], and cut off BG equal to A on BF [1.3].

**Step 3.** Through G, draw GH parallel to BC [1.31].

**Step 4.** Through D, E, and C, draw DK, EL, and CH parallel to BG, meeting GH at K, L, and H respectively [1.31].

**Step 5.** Then BGKD, DKLE, and ELCH are parallelograms, since each has one pair of sides parallel to BG (namely DK, EL, CH) and another pair parallel to BC (namely GK, KL, LH) [by construction via 1.31 and the definition of a parallelogram].

**Step 6.** Now BGHC is a parallelogram with a right angle at B (since BG is at right angles to BC). Since BG equals A [by Step 2], the parallelogram BGHC is the rectangle contained by A and BC [D2.1].

**Step 7.** Consider the parallelogram BGKD. It has a right angle at B, and BG equals A. Therefore BGKD is the rectangle contained by A and BD [D2.1].

**Step 8.** Consider the parallelogram DKLE. Since DK is parallel to BG and BD is parallel to GK (both being segments of parallel lines), the angle at D (angle KDB, formed by DK and the line BC) is a right angle, because BG is perpendicular to BC and DK is parallel to BG, so DK is also perpendicular to BC [1.29]. Furthermore, DK equals BG [1.34], so DK equals A. Therefore DKLE is the rectangle contained by A and DE [D2.1].

**Step 9.** By the same reasoning, EL is parallel to BG, so the angle at E is a right angle [1.29], and EL equals BG equals A [1.34]. Therefore ELCH is the rectangle contained by A and EC [D2.1].

**Step 10.** The rectangle BGHC is manifestly composed of the rectangles BGKD, DKLE, and ELCH, since these three parallelograms partition BGHC without overlap along the base BC. Therefore the rectangle contained by A and BC equals the sum of the rectangles contained by A and BD, A and DE, and A and EC [CN2].

**Step 11.** The same argument applies no matter how many points of division are taken on BC, since for each additional segment we erect a parallel to BG and obtain an additional rectangle with one side equal to A. Therefore, if one of two straight lines be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines equals the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.2
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and both of the segments is equal to the square on the whole.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut at random at point C, so that the segments are AC and CB.

**Step 2.** We must show that rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB) = sq(AB).

**Step 3.** On AB, describe the square ADEB [1.46]. The square on AB is the rectangle contained by AB with itself [D1.22, D2.1].

**Step 4.** Consider AB as two straight lines, both equal to AB, where one of them (AB) is cut into the segments AC and CB. By Proposition 2.1, the rectangle contained by the first line AB and the whole second line AB is equal to the sum of the rectangles contained by the first line AB and each of the segments AC, CB. That is, rect(AB, AB) = rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB) [2.1].

**Step 5.** But rect(AB, AB) is the square on AB [D1.22, D2.1], since the square is the rectangle contained by two equal sides, both equal to AB.

**Step 6.** Therefore, the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment AC together with the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment CB is equal to the square on AB [CN1].

**Step 7.** That is, the rectangle contained by the whole and both of the segments is equal to the square on the whole, which was to be proved. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.3
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut at random at the point C. We must show that the rectangle contained by AB and BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB together with the square on BC.

**Step 2.** Since AB is cut at C, the segments of AB are AC and CB.

**Step 3.** Consider the two straight lines AB and BC. The line AB has been cut into the segments AC and CB. By Proposition 2.1, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines AB and BC is equal to the sum of the rectangles contained by BC and each of the segments of AB. That is, rect(AB, BC) = rect(AC, BC) + rect(CB, BC).

**Step 4.** Now rect(CB, BC) is the rectangle contained by BC and BC, which is the square on BC, since a square is the figure formed when a straight line is multiplied by itself (D2.1, D1.22).

**Step 5.** Therefore rect(AB, BC) = rect(AC, BC) + sq(BC).

**Step 6.** That is, the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BC is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments AC and CB together with the square on the segment BC. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.4
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole is equal to the squares on the segments and twice the rectangle contained by the segments.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut at random at point C, so that the segments are AC and CB. We must show that the square on AB equals the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB.

**Step 2.** By Proposition 2.3, if a straight line AB is cut at C, then the rectangle contained by the whole AB and one segment AC equals the rectangle contained by the segments AC and CB together with the square on AC. That is, rect(AB, AC) = rect(AC, CB) + sq(AC).

**Step 3.** Again by Proposition 2.3, applying it to the segment CB, the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment CB equals the rectangle contained by CB and AC together with the square on CB. That is, rect(AB, CB) = rect(CB, AC) + sq(CB).

**Step 4.** Note that rect(AC, CB) and rect(CB, AC) are the same rectangle (contained by the same two straight lines), so each equals the rectangle contained by the segments.

**Step 5.** Adding the results of Steps 2 and 3 by Common Notion 2, we obtain: rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB) = rect(AC, CB) + sq(AC) + rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB), which is to say rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB) = sq(AC) + sq(CB) + 2 * rect(AC, CB).

**Step 6.** By Proposition 2.2, if a straight line AB is cut at C, the rectangle contained by AB and AC together with the rectangle contained by AB and CB equals the square on AB. That is, rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB) = sq(AB).

**Step 7.** Therefore, by Common Notion 1, the square on AB equals the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB. That is, sq(AB) = sq(AC) + sq(CB) + 2 * rect(AC, CB), which is what was to be proved.

## Proposition 2.5
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut into equal segments at C and into unequal segments at D. We must show that the rectangle contained by AD and DB together with the square on CD equals the square on CB.

**Step 2.** Since CB is cut at the point D, by Proposition 2.4, the square on CB equals the sum of the squares on CD and DB together with twice the rectangle contained by CD and DB. That is, sq(CB) = sq(CD) + sq(DB) + 2*rect(CD, DB).

**Step 3.** Since CB is cut at D, by Proposition 2.3 applied to CB with segment DB, the rectangle contained by CB and DB equals the rectangle contained by CD and DB together with the square on DB. That is, rect(CB, DB) = rect(CD, DB) + sq(DB).

**Step 4.** Now, since AC equals CB (because AB was cut into equal segments at C), the line AD equals AC + CD = CB + CD. Therefore the rectangle contained by AD and DB equals the rectangle contained by (CB + CD) and DB, which by Proposition 2.1 equals rect(CB, DB) + rect(CD, DB).

**Step 5.** Substituting from Step 3 into Step 4, rect(AD, DB) = rect(CD, DB) + sq(DB) + rect(CD, DB) = 2*rect(CD, DB) + sq(DB).

**Step 6.** Adding the square on CD to both sides of the result in Step 5, by Common Notion 2, rect(AD, DB) + sq(CD) = 2*rect(CD, DB) + sq(DB) + sq(CD).

**Step 7.** But from Step 2, sq(CB) = sq(CD) + sq(DB) + 2*rect(CD, DB), which is the same as the right-hand side of Step 6. Therefore, by Common Notion 1, the rectangle contained by AD and DB together with the square on CD equals the square on CB.

**Step 8.** Therefore, if a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 2.6
**Statement:** If a straight line be bisected and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line and the added straight line together with the square on the half is equal to the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line bisected at C, and let BD be added to it in a straight line, so that the points lie in the order A, C, B, D. We must show that the rectangle contained by AD and DB together with the square on CB equals the square on CD.

**Step 2.** On CD, describe the square CEFD, where E lies below C and F below D so that CE is perpendicular to CD. Draw the diagonal DE. [1.46, P1]

**Step 3.** Through B, draw BG parallel to CE, meeting the diagonal DE at H and the side EF at G. Through H, draw LM parallel to CD, meeting CE at L and DF at M. Through A, draw AK parallel to CL, meeting the line through L parallel to AB at the point K. [1.31]

**Step 4.** The rectangle contained by AD and DB is the rectangle ADMK. To see this, note that the side AD runs along the top from A to D, and the side DM runs perpendicular to it. Since BDHM is a parallelogram with BD parallel to MH and BH parallel to DM, we have DM = BH. And since CLHB is a parallelogram with CL parallel to BH, we have BH = CL. Moreover CL is part of CE, which equals CD (side of the square). But LH = CB (since CLHB has CL parallel to BH and CB parallel to LH, making LH = CB), so CL = CE - LE. Now LE = LH = CB (as LEGH is a rectangle with LE perpendicular and LH horizontal, both equal to CB since the diagonal intersects appropriately). Regardless, the perpendicular height from AD down to the line KLM equals BD, because M lies on DF at distance BD below D (since BH is parallel to DM and the vertical distance from B to H equals BD). Hence ADMK has sides AD and DB, confirming it is the rectangle contained by AD and DB.

**Step 5.** The rectangle ADMK is composed of three abutting rectangles arranged left to right: rectangle AL (that is, ACKL), rectangle CH (that is, CLHB), and rectangle CM (that is, BDHM).

**Step 6.** Since AB is bisected at C, we have AC = CB. The parallelograms AL and CH stand on equal bases AC and CB and lie between the same parallels AB and KLM. Therefore AL equals CH in area. [1.36]

**Step 7.** The complements CH and HF about the diagonal DE in the parallelogram CEFD are equal. [1.43]

**Step 8.** From Steps 6 and 7, since AL = CH and CH = HF, we conclude AL = HF. [CN1]

**Step 9.** Now the square CEFD is divided by the lines BG and LM into four rectangles: CH (= CLHB), CM (= BDHM), the rectangle LEGH, and HF (= HGFM). Removing the rectangle LEGH from the square leaves CH + CM + HF, which we call the gnomon.

**Step 10.** Since AL = HF (Step 8), we may substitute AL for HF in the gnomon: the gnomon = CH + CM + HF = CH + CM + AL. But CH + CM + AL is exactly the rectangle ADMK (Step 5), which is the rectangle contained by AD and DB. Therefore the rectangle contained by AD and DB equals the gnomon.

**Step 11.** The rectangle LEGH is the square on CB. For LE is the segment of CE from L down to E: since CL = BD (as CLHB has CB parallel to LH and CL parallel to BH, giving CL = BH; and BDHM has BH = DM, but more directly, L lies on CE at perpendicular distance BD from C, so CL = BD and LE = CE - CL = CD - BD = CB). And EG = CB since G lies on EF at horizontal distance CB from E. Thus LEGH has both sides equal to CB and all angles right, making it the square on CB. [1.46]

**Step 12.** Therefore the square on CD (which is CEFD) equals the gnomon together with the square on CB (which is LEGH). That is, sq(CD) = gnomon + sq(CB). [CN2]

**Step 13.** But we showed in Step 10 that the gnomon equals the rectangle contained by AD and DB. Therefore sq(CD) = rect(AD, DB) + sq(CB), which is to say, the rectangle contained by AD and DB together with the square on CB equals the square on CD. This is what was to be proved.

## Proposition 2.7
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole and that on one of the segments both together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole and the said segment and the square on the remaining segment.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut at random at the point C. We must show that the square on AB together with the square on CB is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB and CB together with the square on AC.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB has been cut at C, by Proposition 2.4, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB. That is, sq(AB) = sq(AC) + sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB).

**Step 3.** Add the square on CB to both sides. By Common Notion 2, sq(AB) + sq(CB) = sq(AC) + sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB). Hence sq(AB) + sq(CB) = sq(AC) + 2·sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB).

**Step 4.** Now, since AB has been cut at C, by Proposition 2.3, the rectangle contained by AB and CB is equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB together with the square on CB. That is, rect(AB, CB) = rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB).

**Step 5.** Therefore twice the rectangle contained by AB and CB equals twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB together with twice the square on CB. That is, 2·rect(AB, CB) = 2·rect(AC, CB) + 2·sq(CB), by Common Notion 2 (adding equals to equals, specifically each quantity to itself).

**Step 6.** From Step 3 we have sq(AB) + sq(CB) = sq(AC) + 2·sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB). From Step 5 we have 2·rect(AB, CB) = 2·rect(AC, CB) + 2·sq(CB). Since the right-hand sides are equal (both equal sq(AC) subtracted from the same quantity — more precisely, both 2·sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB) and 2·rect(AB, CB) are equal by Step 5), we substitute: sq(AB) + sq(CB) = sq(AC) + 2·rect(AB, CB), by Common Notion 1.

**Step 7.** Therefore the square on the whole AB and the square on one of the segments CB, both together, are equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB and CB together with the square on the remaining segment AC. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.8
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, four times the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments together with the square on the remaining segment is equal to the square described on the whole and the aforesaid segment as on one straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line cut at random at point C. Produce AB to D so that BD equals BC [P2, 1.3]. Then AD is the straight line composed of AB and BC (i.e., AB and the segment BC placed in a straight line), and we must show that four times the rectangle contained by AB and BC together with the square on AC equals the square on AD.

**Step 2.** Since BD equals BC, the segment CD is composed of CB and BD, and B is the midpoint of CD, so that CB equals BD.

**Step 3.** Apply Proposition 2.4 to the line AD, which is cut at C into AC and CD: the square on AD equals the square on AC plus the square on CD plus twice the rectangle contained by AC and CD.

**Step 4.** Apply Proposition 2.4 to the line CD, which is cut at B into CB and BD: the square on CD equals the square on CB plus the square on BD plus twice the rectangle contained by CB and BD.

**Step 5.** Since BD equals BC, the square on BD equals the square on CB, and the rectangle contained by CB and BD equals the square on CB [D2.1]. Therefore the square on CD equals the square on CB plus the square on CB plus twice the square on CB, that is, four times the square on CB [CN2].

**Step 6.** Now consider the rectangle contained by AC and CD, where CD is composed of CB and BD. By Proposition 2.1, the rectangle contained by AC and CD equals the rectangle contained by AC and CB plus the rectangle contained by AC and BD.

**Step 7.** Since BD equals BC, the rectangle contained by AC and BD equals the rectangle contained by AC and CB. Therefore the rectangle contained by AC and CD equals twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB [CN2].

**Step 8.** Hence twice the rectangle contained by AC and CD equals four times the rectangle contained by AC and CB.

**Step 9.** Substituting the results of Steps 5 and 8 into Step 3: the square on AD equals the square on AC plus four times the square on CB plus four times the rectangle contained by AC and CB, that is, the square on AD equals the square on AC plus four times (the square on CB plus the rectangle contained by AC and CB) [CN2].

**Step 10.** Apply Proposition 2.3 to the line AB cut at C: the rectangle contained by AB and CB equals the rectangle contained by AC and CB plus the square on CB.

**Step 11.** Therefore four times the rectangle contained by AB and CB equals four times the rectangle contained by AC and CB plus four times the square on CB [CN2].

**Step 12.** By Steps 9 and 11, the square on AD equals the square on AC plus four times the rectangle contained by AB and CB [CN1].

**Step 13.** That is, four times the rectangle contained by AB and BC together with the square on AC equals the square on AD. Since AD is composed of the whole line AB and the segment BC as one straight line, this is the required result. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.9
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the squares on the unequal segments of the whole are double of the square on the half and of the square on the straight line between the points of section.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut into equal segments at C and into unequal segments at D, so that AC = CB. We must show that sq(AD) + sq(DB) = 2·sq(AC) + 2·sq(CD).

**Step 2.** From C, draw CE at right angles to AB [1.11], and cut off CE equal to AC (that is, equal to CB) [1.3].

**Step 3.** Join AE and EB [P1].

**Step 4.** Through D, draw DF parallel to CE, meeting EB at F [1.31]. Through F, draw FG parallel to AB, meeting CE at G [1.31]. Join AF [P1].

**Step 5.** Since AC = CE (by construction) and angle ACE is a right angle (by Step 2), triangle ACE is a right-angled isosceles triangle. Therefore angle CAE = angle CEA, and since the three angles sum to two right angles [1.32], we have angle CAE = angle CEA = half a right angle.

**Step 6.** Similarly, since EC = CB (because CE = AC = CB) and angle ECB is a right angle (being supplementary to angle ACE on the straight line AB, both being right angles [1.13]), triangle ECB is a right-angled isosceles triangle. Therefore angle CEB = angle CBE = half a right angle [1.5, 1.32].

**Step 7.** Since angle CEA = half a right angle and angle CEB = half a right angle, angle AEB = angle CEA + angle CEB = one right angle.

**Step 8.** Since FG is parallel to AB and the straight line CE falls on them, angle EGF = angle ECB = one right angle [1.29].

**Step 9.** In triangle EGF, angle GEF = angle CEB = half a right angle (since F lies on EB and G lies on EC). Since the angles of triangle EGF sum to two right angles [1.32], and angle EGF = one right angle and angle GEF = half a right angle, the remaining angle EFG = half a right angle.

**Step 10.** Since angle GEF = angle EFG (both being half a right angle), the side GF = the side GE [1.6].

**Step 11.** Since DF is parallel to CG and GF is parallel to CD, the figure DGFC is a parallelogram. Therefore DF = GC and CD = GF [1.34].

**Step 12.** Since CD = GF (Step 11) and GF = GE (Step 10), we have GE = CD.

**Step 13.** Now CE = AC (by construction), and GE = CD (Step 12), so GC = CE - GE = AC - CD. Also DB = CB - CD = AC - CD (since AC = CB). Therefore GC = DB, and hence DF = DB (since DF = GC by Step 11).

**Step 14.** In right triangle ACE (right angle at C), by the Pythagorean theorem, sq(AE) = sq(AC) + sq(CE) [1.47]. Since AC = CE, this gives sq(AE) = 2·sq(AC).

**Step 15.** In right triangle EGF (right angle at G, by Step 8), sq(EF) = sq(EG) + sq(GF) [1.47]. Since EG = GF (Step 10), this gives sq(EF) = 2·sq(GF) = 2·sq(CD) (since GF = CD by Step 11).

**Step 16.** In triangle AEF, since angle AEF = angle AEB = one right angle (Step 7, and F lies on EB), by the Pythagorean theorem, sq(AF) = sq(AE) + sq(EF) [1.47].

**Step 17.** Since DF is parallel to CE and CE is perpendicular to AB, the angle ADF is a right angle [1.29]. In right triangle ADF, sq(AF) = sq(AD) + sq(DF) [1.47].

**Step 18.** From Steps 16 and 17, sq(AE) + sq(EF) = sq(AD) + sq(DF) [CN1].

**Step 19.** Since DF = DB (Step 13), sq(DF) = sq(DB), so sq(AE) + sq(EF) = sq(AD) + sq(DB).

**Step 20.** From Steps 14 and 15, sq(AE) + sq(EF) = 2·sq(AC) + 2·sq(CD).

**Step 21.** Therefore sq(AD) + sq(DB) = 2·sq(AC) + 2·sq(CD) [CN1]. That is, the squares on the unequal segments of the whole are double of the square on the half and of the square on the straight line between the points of section. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 2.10
**Statement:** If a straight line be bisected, and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the square on the whole with the added straight line and the square on the added straight line both together are double of the square on the half and of the square described on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line as on one straight line.

By 2.6, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line (that is, AD) and the added straight line (DB), together with the square on the half (CB), equals the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line (CD). That is: rect(AD, DB) + sq(CB) = sq(CD).

Now rect(AC, AC) = sq(AC) [by the definition of a square, D2.1 and D1.22]. Therefore sq(AB) = 2*sq(AC) + 2*sq(AC) = 4*sq(AC) [CN2].

**Step 6.** Similarly, since the angle at D is right, triangle BCD is right-angled at D. By the Pythagorean theorem, the square on BC equals the squares on CD and DB together: sq(BC) = sq(CD) + sq(DB) [1.47].
